title: Functions and expressions
summary: Parameters in, one value out, and why the last line has no semicolon.

blocks.html: A function is a name for a piece of work. Every parameter carries an explicit type, and the return type follows an arrow. Nothing about a signature is inferred: fn name(parameter: Type) -> Type is the whole shape, and a function that returns nothing simply omits the arrow.

blocks.title: one parameter, one result

blocks.html:
Look closely at the body: n * 2 has no semicolon. The body is a block, and a block is an expression whose value is its last line. With -> i32 promised, that final value is what the function hands back.

A line that ends in a semicolon is a statement: it does something and yields nothing. A line without one is an expression: it has a value.

blocks.title: the semicolon that eats the answer

blocks.html:
That semicolon turns the answer into a statement, so the body has no value left to return. The compiler says error[E0308]: mismatched types, notes that it expected i32, found (), and adds help: remove this semicolon to return this value. The () is the empty tuple: the type of a block that produces nothing.

If you ever see expected i32, found (), hunt for a stray semicolon on the last line of the function.

Because blocks are expressions, a block can be used anywhere a value goes, including the right side of a let. Inside the braces you may run as many statements as you like; the last line without a semicolon supplies the value for the whole block.

blocks.title: a block as a value

blocks.html: The trailing expression is the normal way to return a value, and it is the one you should reach for. return still exists for early exit: guard clauses at the top of a function that bail out before the real work. Both styles in one function read well — return for the exception, a trailing expression for the rule.

blocks.title: return for the early exit
a function that calls a function

blocks.html: Functions call each other freely: total uses with_tax as if it were a value, because a call is an expression. That is how programs get built — a few small functions with type-checked contracts, and one main that wires them together. Note that price * 121 / 100 stays in integers, so the tax is truncated to whole units.

quiz.why: The body must end in an expression of the promised type. A trailing semicolon leaves the empty tuple, and a missing -> i32 promises nothing at all.

quiz.q: In a function signature, what always needs a type written out?
quiz.why: Parameter types are mandatory because the compiler will not guess across a function boundary. Local bindings inside the body are usually inferred from their initializer.

quiz.q: What is the value of the block { let a = 2; a * 3 }
quiz.why: A block is an expression whose value is its last line, here a * 3. The let above it is a statement, so it contributes nothing.

exercise.brief: Write a function total that takes two i32 parameters and returns their sum, then print the result of total(4, 5) from main.
exercise.hint: The signature is fn total(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32. The body can be a single expression with no semicolon: a + b.
